verses.text: Morning came, and all the chief priests and elders held a meeting. They agreed Jesus had to die.
They tied him up, took him away, and handed him over to Governor Pontius Pilate.
Judas, the one who betrayed Jesus, saw he’d been condemned. Regret hit him hard; he brought the thirty silver coins back to the chief priests and elders.
“I sinned,” he said. “I handed over an innocent man.” They replied, “That’s your problem. What’s it to us?”
Judas threw the silver into the temple sanctuary, walked out, and went and hanged himself.
The chief priests picked up the coins. “We can’t put this in the treasury; it’s blood money.”
They talked it over, then used the money to buy the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers.
That’s why, to this day, people call it “Field of Blood.”
That fulfilled what Jeremiah the prophet had said: “They took the thirty silver coins—the price some of Israel’s people put on him—
and used them to buy the potter’s field, just as the Lord directed me.”
Jesus stood in front of the governor. Pilate asked, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus replied, “Those are your words.”
The chief priests and elders accused him, but he didn’t answer them.
Pilate asked, “You hearing all these charges they’re bringing against you?”
Jesus didn’t answer even one charge, and the governor was seriously surprised.
At the festival, the governor had a tradition: he’d release one prisoner, whoever the crowd chose.
Right then they had a notorious prisoner named Barabbas.
When the crowd gathered, Pilate asked, “Who should I release for you—Barabbas, or Jesus, the one called Christ?”
Pilate knew they’d handed Jesus over because jealousy was driving them.
While Pilate sat on the judge’s seat, his wife sent a message: “Leave that righteous man alone. I had a terrible dream about him today.”
Meanwhile, the chief priests and elders worked the crowd, telling them to ask for Barabbas and have Jesus killed.
The governor asked, “Which one of these two do you want me to release?” They shouted, “Barabbas!”
Pilate said, “Then what should I do with Jesus, the one called Christ?” The whole crowd yelled, “Crucify him!”
He asked, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they only shouted louder: “Crucify him!”
Pilate saw he wasn’t getting anywhere and a riot was about to break out. He washed his hands in front of everyone: “I’m innocent of this righteous man’s blood. That’s on you.”
All the people answered, “Let his blood be on us and on our children!”
Then Pilate released Barabbas. He had Jesus whipped and handed over for crucifixion.
The governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium and gathered the whole troop around him.
They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him.
They twisted thorn branches into a crown and put it on his head. Then they put a reed in his right hand, knelt in front of him, and mocked him: “Hail, King of the Jews!”
They spat on him, grabbed the reed, and kept striking his head with it.
After all that mockery, they took off the robe, put his own clothes back on, and led him away to crucify him.
As they headed out, they found Simon from Cyrene and forced him to carry Jesus’ cross.
They arrived at Golgotha, a place whose name means “Place of a Skull.”
They offered Jesus wine mixed with gall. He tasted it, but wouldn’t drink.
After they crucified him, they divided his clothes among themselves by throwing dice.
Then they sat down and kept watch over him.
They posted the charge over his head: “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
Two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.
People passing by hurled insults at him and shook their heads.
“You said you’d tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days. Save yourself! If you’re God’s Son, come down from that cross!”
The chief priests, legal teachers, Pharisees, and elders joined in mocking him:
“He saved other people, but look at him now—he can’t save himself! If he’s Israel’s King, let him come down from the cross right now. Then we’ll believe him.
“He trusts God, right? Let God rescue him now, if God wants him. He said, ‘I am God’s Son.’”
Even the robbers crucified beside him threw the same insults at him.
From noon until three, darkness covered the whole land.
About three o’clock, Jesus cried out loudly, “Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?” That means, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?”
Some people standing there heard him and said, “He’s calling Elijah.”
One of them ran straight away, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink.
The others said, “Hold up. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to save him.”
Jesus cried out loudly once more, then gave up his spirit.
At that moment, the temple curtain ripped in two from top to bottom. The earth shook, and rocks split apart.
Tombs opened, and many bodies of God’s holy people who had died were raised to life.
After Jesus was raised, they came out of their tombs, entered the holy city, and appeared to many people.
The centurion and the soldiers guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and everything happening. They were terrified and said, “This really was God’s Son!”
Many women were there too, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee and cared for him.
Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee’s sons.
As evening came, a rich man named Joseph from Arimathaea arrived. He was also Jesus’ disciple.
He went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. Pilate ordered them to hand it over.
Joseph took the body and wrapped it in clean linen.
He laid it in his own new tomb, cut into the rock. Then he rolled a big stone across the entrance and left.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary stayed there, sitting across from the tomb.
The next day—the day after Preparation Day—the chief priests and Pharisees came together before Pilate.
“Sir,” they said, “we remember that while that deceiver was still alive, he said, ‘After three days I’ll rise again.’

“So give the order to secure the tomb until the third day. Otherwise his disciples could come at night, steal him, and tell everyone, ‘He rose from the dead.’ Then this last deception would be worse than the first.”
Pilate told them, “You have a guard. Go make it as secure as you know how.”
They went with the guard, secured the tomb, and sealed the stone.
